query_preview:
..Quiet day across all of Southeast Arizona today
with sunny skies and light winds observed across the area. The 
upper pattern early this afternoon is defined by an upper trough
across the Pacific Northwest and the northern portions of the
Intermountain West, a strong upper-low in the Eastern pacific
near 33N/147W, and a generalized zonal flow extending from this
feature into the Desert Southwest. The latest GOES precipitable
water imagery indicated a dry airmass across our neck of the
woods, ranging from 0.25-0.45 inches. 

An upper ridge building into the Gulf of Alaska will try to 
phase the upper-low in the NW with the EPAC low, resulting in 
an amplified mean trough. Strong northerly flow developing on 
the backside of this trough will help weaken the closed 
circulation over the Eastern Pacific, eventually allowing this 
system to open into a progressive the second half of the week. 
This feature will weaken as it moves east, but southerly low to 
mid-level flow developing out ahead of the trough should 
encourage a northward surge of tropical moisture (the extreme 
northerly extent of Hurricane Vance) through the Gulf of 
California and into southwest Arizona Thursday night into 
Friday. The 26/12Z deterministic GFS indicated decent 700-850mb 
moisture flux convergence west and northwest of Tucson between 
30/18Z and 31/00Z Friday. Expect scattered showers and 
thunderstorms as early as Thursday night but more likely during 
the day Friday across Southeast Arizona with this moisture push.
Rainfall amounts will generally be a tenth to third inch across
the majority of the CWA with this first system. However, given 
the fact the N/S orientation of the moisture plume aligns with 
the stronger southerly low-level flow, we may see areas where 
training of storms may increase the potential for heavier 
rainfall amounts across central and western Pima/SE Pinal 
counties Friday. 

The aforementioned ridging in the Gulf of Alaska will then push
another shortwave south, reinforcing the mean trough over the
Eastern Pacific late Friday into Saturday. This will close off 
another upper-low near 27N/130W by 01/00Z Saturday afternoon 
before shifting this feature east toward Arizona Sunday. This 
low will tap into a deep plume of subtropical moisture as it 
makes its way into Arizona with the GEFS still indicating PWATs
in this plume 2.5 to 3.0 standard deviations above normal.
Examining both the 26/12Z GEFS and ECMWF ensemble data with 
respect to an atmospheric river event thru the Center for 
Western Weather and Water Extremes, the mean IVT for this second
event Sunday is very close to 500 kg/ms which would lean it 
toward an AR2 event, but the shorter duration (around 24 hours) 
of the moisture plume limits the event more toward and AR1 
scale classification. In any event, this is looking like it will
be a heavy precipitation event for Arizona, with the strong 
SWLY flow likely focusing the heaviest precipitation into 
central AZ and especially the Mogollon Rim Sunday with strong 
orographic lift. The northern portions of our CWA including SE 
Pinal, Graham and Greenlee counties will be the main focus in 
Southeast Arizona.

In general, moderate-intensity rainfall will produce a half to 
one inch of storm-total (Sunday and Monday) rainfall in the 
valleys, with amounts between 1 to 2 inches in the mountains. 
Heavier amounts to 2.50 inches will be possible on the SW facing
slopes of the higher terrain from Tucson north and northeast 
including the Catalina and Rincon Mountains. Since the rainfall 
is occuring over a longer duration of time, I anticipate rainfall
runoff will result in water flowing within normally dry washes 
and roadway dips with significant ponding of water in low-lying 
and poor drainage areas possible. Heavy flows may be present in 
creeks and rivers across northern Graham and Greenlee counties 
like the San Francisco, Blue and even Gila rivers, potentially 
impacting localized areas into early next week depending on the 
magnitude of the rainfall event.

I guess the good news for the kiddos is that at this time, it 
still looks like Halloween may be the lull in storm activity in 
between these two distinct weather systems Friday and 
Sunday...but timing can change, and residual moisture and 
generalized instability may result in a low-end chance of 
showers.
